title: Honi sleeps seventy years (Taanit 23a)
hook: he wakes to find no one knows him, and says: companionship or death

segments.voice: Yesterday, two in the desert, one flask. Your line was your life comes first. Did you refill your own flask? Today we go back to Honi and his carob tree. Day two hundred eighty-six.

You've probably had a tiny version of this. You come back from a long trip, or a long illness, or years away, and the old group chat has moved on without you. The inside jokes are new. Someone else sits in your chair. You walk into the room and nobody quite knows where to put you. Last week we met Honi, the circle-drawer, watching an old man plant a carob tree for his grandchildren. The Talmud says that the very same day, Honi sat down to eat, and fell asleep.
screen: `THE GROUP CHAT MOVED ON.` → `SOMEONE ELSE IN YOUR CHAIR.` → `HONI SITS DOWN TO EAT.`

segments.voice: The Talmud says Honi had puzzled all his life over a line from the Psalms about the return from exile: "we were like unto them that dream." Seventy years of exile, like a dream? How could anyone sleep seventy years? Now, after meeting the old planter, he sits down to eat, sleep overtakes him, and rocks grow up around him and hide him. He sleeps for seventy years. When he wakes, he sees a man gathering carobs from a tree. Are you the one who planted this? No, the man says, I'm his grandson. Honi goes home and asks for his son. His son has died; his grandson is alive. He goes to the study house and hears the scholars say: these teachings are as clear as in the days of Honi, because when he came here, he'd answer every question. He tells them: I am Honi. They don't believe him. They don't give him the respect he's used to. The Talmud says he was deeply hurt, and asked for mercy, and died. And then a sage named Rava sums it up with a saying people used: either companionship, or death. In Aramaic, o chavruta, o mituta. It's the saddest story on that page, and the Talmud tells it plainly. A person can have wisdom, fame, and answered prayers. Without people who know you, it isn't a life. That's what Honi learned when he woke.
screen: `WE WERE LIKE THEM THAT DREAM.` · `SEVENTY YEARS ASLEEP.` · `NO ONE KNOWS HIM.` · `COMPANIONSHIP, OR DEATH.` · then, large: `FRIENDSHIP OR DEATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wake up an old friendship. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who used to know you well, and whom you've drifted from. A school friend. An old roommate. A cousin. A former coworker you really liked. Let their face come. Remember one thing you laughed about together. Now picture sending them one short message today. Nothing big. Thought of you. How are you? That's all. The bell holds the time.
Honi sleeps seventy years. He wakes to a world where no one knows him, and the Talmud says: either companionship, or death.
Your line: friendship or death. Today, reach out to one old companion, even with three words. Day two hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Jewish study is traditionally done with a chavruta, a study partner, a word from the same root as Rava's saying; the story of Honi's sleep is often told to explain why learning alone is not enough.

what it means: without people who know you, even a great life isn't a life.
what a scholar hears: chavruta, from chaver, friend, became the word for a study partner, and the story explains Psalm 126's seventy-year dream.

notes: Taanit 23a paraphrased. The Talmud connects Psalm 126 to the seventy years of the Babylonian exile.
Honi's asking for mercy and dying is told plainly and briefly; a Keeper may want to review the tone of this sensitive detail.
Check JPS 1917 Psalm 126:1 ('We were like unto them that dream').
A different version of Honi's death appears in Josephus (Onias, stoned during a civil war); not mentioned.
